newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Insurers fear growth of 'compensation culture'.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Insurers fear growth of 'compensation culture'.

text.p: Insurers fear a growing "compensation culture" in which almost anyone feels they can sue for damages from almost anything, regardless of whether the plaintiffs contributed to their own injury.

Friday's landmark deal to settle tobacco litigation in the United States has emphasised the huge risks insurers could face from individual lawsuits, class actions and government-sponsored action related to a range of products from alcohol, to cars and drugs.
The financial impact of the $368 billion tobacco settlement on insurers is not yet clear.
But the message it sends to the world -- that litigation works -- will have major ramifications on the task of underwriting liability insurance in the future.

Catastrophe insurers take great care to monitor their exposure to any one event -- analysing their account by zones, modelling past events and theoretical events in the future, to see what they would cost in insured damage.
They can then build into the price of their products a charge which allows for an assumed catastrophe of a certain size to happen once every so many years.

But liability insurers find it impossible to make predictions based on averages or models, especially in the current environment where they are often seen as soft 'deep pocket' targets for even the most unlikely litigation.
GROWING COMPENSATION CULTURE
Lloyd's underwriter Stephen Burnhope sees a growing "compensation culture".
"This is a way of thinking that says if you have suffered harm, bodily or financially, then it's someone else's fault, not your fault, and you ought to be compensated," said Burnhope.

"Over time, the inroads made by this compensation culture have eroded personal responsibility and the recognition that life itself involves a degree of risk assumption; that investment and commerce can result in failure and loss, as well as success and profit," said Burnhope, adding: "The fact is, bad stuff sometimes happens to good people for no reason."
INSURANCE AS INCOME REDISTRIBUTION
Like other insurers Burnhope fears that a "right to be compensated" is being established in some jurisdictions.
Just as governments redistribute the wealth of the fortunate to those less well off, society is increasingly accepting a similar approach by the judicial system.
The concern is that loss becomes directly linked to an expectation of compensation being paid, and that 'fault' becomes merely a mechanism for establishing who will pay.

"The courts themselves have no fund from which to pay financial compensation, so it's tempting to redistribute from those in favour of those who have not, while neatly side-stepping the moral issue involved," said Burnhope.
An example of Burnhope's concerns is given by Richard Neely, a justice of the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals and Professor of Economics at the University of Charleston.
In his book "The Product Liability Mess" he wrote:

"The anarchy that currently prevails among American state jurisdictions absolutely guarantees politically that no line of any sort will ever be drawn. After all, I'm not the only appellate judge in America who wants to sleep at night. As long as I am allowed to redistribute wealth from the out-of-state companies to injured plaintiffs, I shall continue to do so," he wrote.
"Not only is my sleep enhanced when I give someone else's money away, but so is my job security, because the in-state plaintiffs, their families, and their friends will re-elect me."
It is this kind of thinking which encourages mass legal actions and terrifies insurers.
INSURERS ON THE OFFENSIVE
Some U.S. insurers recommend taking the offensive.

At an insurance conference last week Michael Furlong of Employers Re in Kansas said that when claims raise a red flag to the possibility of a mass action, insurers should create a 'no mercy' perception and fight cases to the very end.
"It behoves insurers to pick the right battle. Don't go to trial against the best claimant's attorney, choose which cases you want to try first," he said.
However a note of caution comes from David McIntosh, senior partner with London insurance law firm Davies Arnold Cooper.
"Experience has shown that even cases which are doubtful on their merits can be too costly to even succeed within a court system where the winners costs are not paid by the loser," he says.

The lead for the growth of the "litigious society" comes clearly from the United States where numbers of lawsuits and class actions have been on the rise for some time. But the phenomenon is becoming global.
Britain is leading a European trend in the growth of personal injury claims and the establishment of "no win, no fee" plaintiff law firms encouraging people to "have a go" at winning compensation.

An escalation of insurance disputes is also predicted in Asia. Last month Mark Kennan, a partner with the U.S. law firm Anderson Kill & Olick, told Reuters: "I don't know necessarily that there will be that mass tort type claim where every smoker sues every tobacco company or manufacturer in the area, but I believe litigation problems in Asia will happen very quickly."

He said commercial contract disputes and personal lines liability claims would be the key drivers of litigation. Another lawyer feared product liability claims in Asia are being driven by "a get rich quick" motive.

The tobacco litigation has explored new legal theories that could lead to class action lawsuits for other products that are proven health hazards, such as alcohol. Pharmaceuticals, genetically-altered drugs and environmental hazards such as formaldehyde in building materials are other potential targets for mass litigation.

They have the same distinguishing characteristics as other class actions -- thousands of potential claimants, solvent and well insured defendants, and scientific evidence that there is a direct relationship between the use of the product and damage.
ACTS OF MAN, NOT ACTS OF GOD
The insurance industry is also concerned about other issues which could lead to a raft of litigation against liability insurers.
David McIntosh has list of phenomenons of modern society he believes will be used by proactive plaintiff lawyers to access insurers assets.
"It is Acts of Man, not Acts of God which are now the bigger risk," says McIntosh.
The list covers all aspects of life.

The millennium computer bug could lead to actions against company directors, accountants and consultants, IT suppliers and the like if systems malfunction on 1 January 2000. One U.S. lawyer estimated this could lead to $1 trillion worth of litigation, more than asbestos, pollution and other previous liabilities put together.
Computer hacking and virus introduction may lead to negligence claims alleging shortcomings in computer security, while Internet copyright and libel litigation has yet to be explored.
The Dow Corning silicon breast implant action and the resulting bankruptcy of the company opened the way for claims against other medical manufacturers.
Medical malpractice suits continue to plague hospitals, particularly in the U.S. where a recent study found 80 percent of claims against doctors in New York were without merit

And environmental clean-up poses a threat, especially the risk of major environmental catastrophe in a heavily built-up area. Insurers fear they will also be made to pay for cleaning up Eastern Europe.

"All of these 'New Age' cases will invariably ensnare company directors, officers and all other professionals. This will add to the size of an already massive financial litigation iceberg threatening consequences of Titanic proportion," said McIntosh.
GOVERNMENTS AS PLAINTIFF
Perhaps the biggest fear highlighted by Friday's tobacco settlement, where U.S. state authorities were the plaintiffs, is the growth of government units as plaintiffs.

Insurers predict that the regulatory arms of government, whether environmental agencies or financial watchdogs will increasingly take the initiative in bringing or supporting attempts to recover money from big business and its advisors.
Burnhope points to lessons learned in the Savings and Loans debacle in the U.S. in the late 1980's.

"Government agencies represent very powerful and very dangerous plaintiffs. The defence of those claims was complicated by the plaintiff's lack of economic discipline in expending legal costs and unpredictable case management in the way attorneys were supervised," he said.
"Commercial settlements proved difficult to negotiate because of a lack of commercial incentive to settle, compared to the politically driven need to achieve an acceptable result," he added.

The latest indications from the U.S., which indicate that the tobacco deal is being scrutinised by federal and public health bodies and that even tougher conditions may be sought, will do nothing to ease insurance industry concerns.
